b: No. Reports mention that he also accepted pledges from children such as al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Abbās, 'Abd Allāh ibn Ja'far, 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, and 'Abd Allāh ibn Ja'far while they were still young.

f: Does the reported evidence indicate that a person may give bay'ah more than once?
b: Yes. 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr reported, "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ twice in one day," indicating that renewing the pledge is permissible.

f: Do the Naqshbandī shaykhs claim extraordinary authority in training disciples?
b: No. They train disciples only according to their ability and capacity.

f: According to what principle do the shaykhs train disciples?
b: They train them according to their ability and capacity (حَسَبَ الطَّاقَةِ وَالْإِمْكَانِ).

f: Which Qur'anic principle supports training people according to their ability?
b: "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity." (Qur'an 2:286)

f: Which Qur'anic verse commands fearing Allah according to one's ability?
b: "So fear Allah as much as you are able." (Qur'an 64:16)

f: How did the Prophet ﷺ qualify the pledge of obedience taken from his Companions?
b: He would say, "As much as you are able (فِيمَا اِسْتَطَعْتُمْ)."

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to the women when accepting their pledge of allegiance?
b: He accepted their pledge "according to what you are able and capable of."

f: How is the covenant (ʿahd) with the shaykh physically initiated?
b: The disciple sits in a state of ritual purity (wuḍū'), sits before the shaykh, and places his hand in the shaykh's hand.

f: What declaration does the disciple make when taking the covenant?
b: "This is Allah's covenant between me and you upon the Qur'an and the Sunnah."

f: What commitment regarding major sins does the disciple make during the covenant?
b: He pledges not to commit any major sin.

f: What commitment regarding minor sins does the disciple make during the covenant?
b: He pledges not to persist in any minor sin.

f: What must a disciple do if he falls into sin after taking the covenant?
b: He must hasten to repent and remove the burden of that sin through sincere repentance.

f: What obligations regarding worship does the disciple pledge to fulfill?
b: He pledges to remain steadfast in the obligatory acts of worship and to persevere in the voluntary acts of worship.

f: What approach to religious practice does the disciple pledge to adopt?
b: He pledges to act upon the stricter course ('azīmah) and to avoid unnecessary reliance upon concessions (rukhaṣ) and innovations (bid'ah).

f: How does the covenant describe the relationship between the shaykh and the disciple?
b: They are brothers for the sake of Allah, and whoever is saved will take his brother by the hand on the Day of Resurrection.

f: To whom do the Naqshbandī disciples trace their spiritual affiliation in this covenant?
b: To the Imam of the path and spiritual master, Khwājah Bahā' al-Dīn Naqshband Muḥammad al-Uwaysī al-Bukhārī.

f: What does the shaykh require from the disciple regarding his past sins before completing the covenant?
b: The shaykh has him repent from all the sins and acts of disobedience committed throughout his life.

f: Which formula of repentance is recited during the covenant, and how many times?
b: "Astaghfirullāh alladhī lā ilāha illā Huwa al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm wa atūbu ilayh" ("I seek forgiveness from Allah, besides Whom there is no deity, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I repent to Him.") is recited three times.

f: What is recited once after the pledge (bayʿah) for blessing?
b: The shaykh recites once: "Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. The Hand of Allah is over their hands. Whoever breaks his pledge only breaks it against himself, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, He will grant him a tremendous reward." (Qur'an 48:10).

f: What do the shaykh and the murīd do immediately after reciting Qur'an 48:10?
b: They both place their hands on their knees, close their eyes, and the shaykh silently remembers the Divine Name (Ism al-Dhāt) in his heart three times with the intention of instructing and transmitting it to the murīd's heart.

f: What is meant by Ism al-Dhāt in this context?
b: It refers to the Divine Name "Allah", remembered for the purpose of purification of the heart, directing it toward its Creator, and cultivating sincerity after taking the covenant.

f: Which Qur'anic verses are cited as evidence for remembering the Divine Name?
b: Among them are: "Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him completely." (73:8), "Remember the name of your Lord morning and evening." (76:25), "Successful is the one who purifies himself, remembers the name of his Lord, and prays." (87:14–15), and "Say: Allah, then leave them in their vain discourse." (6:91).

f: Which hadith indicates that the Hour will not come until the remembrance of Allah disappears from the earth?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The Hour will not be established until it is no longer said on the earth: 'Allah, Allah.'" Another narration states: "until 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh' is no longer said."

f: Which hadith shows Allah's nearness to the servant who remembers Him?
b: The Prophet ﷺ narrated that Allah says: "I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move with My remembrance."

f: What qualification does the commentary make regarding saying only the word "Allah" in dhikr?
b: The more complete practice is that saying "Allah" should not be devoid of an intended meaning in the heart, such as an implied supplication, glorification, or declaration of His oneness, even if that meaning is not verbally expressed.

f: Why should someone not be criticized merely for repeating the single word "Allah" in dhikr?
b: Because the intention of the heart is unknown, Muslims are commanded to think well of others, and one cannot judge what is hidden in the hearts.

f: How does the commentary answer the objection that the single word "Allah" does not form a complete sentence?
b: It replies that the person remembering Allah is not addressing human beings who require a complete linguistic statement; rather, he is remembering Allah, who knows what is hidden and what is even more concealed.

f: According to the narration from Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ cited by Ibn ʿĀbidīn, what is Allah's Greatest Name (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam)?
b: The Name "Allah" itself is Allah's Greatest Name.

f: Which scholars are mentioned as holding that "Allah" is the Greatest Name?
b: Abu Hanifah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, al-Kisāʾī, al-Shaʿbī, Ismāʿīl ibn Isḥāq, Abū Ḥafṣ, and the majority of scholars.

f: What do the majority of Sufi masters and realized gnostics believe regarding the remembrance of the Name "Allah"?
b: They hold that "Allah" is the Greatest Name and that there is no higher form of dhikr for one who has attained the spiritual station of remembering Allah by His Name alone.

f: What supplication does ʿAbd al-Majīd al-Khānī recommend saying at the beginning of the dhikr of the Divine Name?
b: "My God, You are my goal, and Your good pleasure is what I seek." It is said at the beginning of the dhikr and at the start of every hundred repetitions.

f: What is the purpose of saying, "My God, You are my goal, and Your good pleasure is what I seek"?
b: To keep the heart attached to seeking Allah's pleasure and to ensure that the remembrance of His Name is not empty of sincere intention, while contemplating Allah as though one sees Him (iḥsān).

f: After the shaykh silently remembers the Divine Name three times, what does the murīd do?
b: The murīd also remembers the Divine Name silently in his heart three times with the intention of receiving the instruction (talqīn).

f: Is the method of giving talqīn (instruction in dhikr) restricted to one fixed form?
b: No. The method is not limited to a specific wording, posture, action, or movement. It may be adapted according to what best benefits the seeker, strengthens concentration, and preserves proper etiquette.

f: Which Qur'anic verses are cited as evidence for the principle of talqīn (instruction)?
b: Among them are: "Then Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ received words from his Lord..." (2:37), "Know that there is no deity except Allah." (47:19), and "O you who believe, remember Allah with abundant remembrance and glorify Him morning and evening." (33:41–42).

f: What Sunnah concludes the session after the talqīn?
b: The shaykh and the murīd raise their hands together in supplication, and the shaykh prays for the murīd.

f: Which Prophetic practice supports ending gatherings with duʿāʾ?
b: Ibn ʿUmar رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا reported that the Prophet ﷺ rarely left a gathering without supplicating for his companions, asking Allah for fear of Him, obedience, certainty, well-being, victory over enemies, and protection from worldly distractions.

f: What supplication did the Prophet ﷺ frequently say at the end of gatherings as an expiation for mistakes?
b: "Subḥānaka Allāhumma wa biḥamdik, astaghfiruka wa atūbu ilayk" ("Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise is Yours. I seek Your forgiveness and repent to You.").

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about reciting the expiatory supplication before leaving a gathering?
b: Whoever says it before leaving a gathering in which there was idle or excessive speech will have what occurred in that gathering forgiven.

f: What do the shaykh and the murīd do after completing the supplication?
b: They wipe their hands over their faces.

f: What does the murīd do after wiping his face?
b: He kisses the shaykh's knee, stands up, receives permission to leave, and occupies himself with the instructions the shaykh has given him.

f: What is expected of the murīd after taking the covenant?
b: He should preserve his bond with the shaykh in all circumstances, remain faithful to the covenant and pledge, and never break it until death.

f: What is meant by the negation and affirmation (al-nafy wa al-ithbāt) in dhikr?
b: It refers to the statement "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" ("There is no deity except Allah").

f: How is the talqīn of Lā ilāha illā Allāh performed?
b: It is performed in the same manner as the talqīn of the Divine Name, except that during the talqīn both the shaykh and the murīd hold their breath while giving and receiving the instruction.

f: What narration does the book cite regarding the talqīn of Lā ilāha illā Allāh to ʿAlī?
b: It reports that ʿAlī asked the Prophet ﷺ for the shortest and easiest path to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ instructed him to close his eyes, listen while the Prophet ﷺ recited "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" three times, then repeat it three times while the Prophet ﷺ listened.

f: Which hadith is cited to support raising the hands while saying Lā ilāha illā Allāh?
b: Shaddād ibn Aws reported that the Prophet ﷺ asked those present to raise their hands and say "Lā ilāha illā Allāh." After they did so, he praised Allah and said, "Rejoice, for Allah has forgiven you."

f: What meaning should be kept in mind while reciting Lā ilāha illā Allāh, according to ʿAbd al-Majīd al-Khānī?
b: The dhikr should be accompanied by the awareness that there is no true goal or object of seeking except Allah Himself.

f: What additional practice distinguishes the talqīn of Lā ilāha illā Allāh from the talqīn of the Divine Name?
b: During the talqīn of Lā ilāha illā Allāh, both the shaykh and the murīd hold their breath while giving and receiving the instruction.

f: What is dhikr defined as?
b: Dhikr is the repeated remembrance of the One remembered (Allah) upon the heart and the tongue.

f: How does the author describe the obligation of dhikr?
b: He describes it as a necessary and perpetual obligation.

f: Which Qur'anic verse is cited as the foundation for Allah remembering those who remember Him?
b: "So remember Me; I will remember you." (Qur'an 2:152)

f: What does the hadith qudsī cited here say about Allah's response to those who remember Him?
b: Allah says: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me privately, I remember him privately; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in a better assembly. If he draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by an arm's length; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running."

f: Which deed did the Prophet ﷺ describe as better than spending gold and silver and even fighting in Allah's cause?
b: The remembrance of Allah (dhikr).

f: According to Muʿādh ibn Jabal, what is the greatest protection from Allah's punishment?
b: Nothing saves a person from Allah's punishment more than the remembrance of Allah.

f: How is "Remember Me; I will remember you" explained in one narration from Ibn ʿAbbās?
b: "Remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with forgiveness."

f: What statement from Ibn ʿAbbās is cited regarding Allah's remembrance of His servants?
b: "Allah's remembrance of you is greater than your remembrance of Him."

f: According to the hadith qudsī cited from Abū Hurayrah, what does remembering or forgetting Allah signify?
b: Allah says: "O son of Adam عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, when you remember Me, you have thanked Me; when you forget Me, you have shown ingratitude to Me."

f: What did Allah tell Mūsā when he asked how to thank Him properly?
b: "Remember Me and do not forget Me. If you remember Me, you have thanked Me; if you forget Me, you have been ungrateful to Me."

f: Which four blessings are linked together in the narration of Ibn Masʿūd?
b: Whoever is granted dhikr is granted Allah's remembrance; whoever is granted duʿāʾ is granted an answer; whoever is granted gratitude (shukr) is granted increase; and whoever is granted istighfār is granted forgiveness.

f: How does the author describe dhikr for the spiritual seeker (murīd)?
b: It is the sword of the seekers, the fortress of those who remember Allah, and the charter or seal of sainthood (wilāyah).

f: What does the author say about the one who is granted constant dhikr?
b: He has been granted the charter of sainthood (wilāyah).

f: What does the author say about the one who abandons dhikr?
b: He has been removed from that charter of sainthood.

f: How does the author describe dhikr in relation to the spiritual path?
b: It is the measure of union with Allah, the sign of the light of the final goal, the nearest path to arrival, and the best deed for acceptance.

f: According to the author, where do all virtuous qualities originate?
b: All praiseworthy qualities ultimately return to Allah, and their source is dhikr.

f: Which Qur'anic verse concludes this section on the superiority of dhikr?
b: "And the remembrance of Allah is greater." (Qur'an 29:45)

f: What is the greatest honor of dhikr mentioned by the author?
b: Its reward is that Allah remembers the one who remembers Him, as in the verse: "So remember Me; I will remember you." (Qur'an 2:152).

f: How does Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explain the verse "Remember Me; I will remember you"?
b: Remember Me through obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness.

f: How did al-Qurṭubī explain the structure of the verse "Remember Me; I will remember you"?
b: It is a command followed by its response, expressing reciprocal recompense: remembering Allah through obedience is met by Allah's remembrance through reward and forgiveness.

f: What did Abū ʿAlī al-Daqqāq say about dhikr and wilāyah?
b: Dhikr is the charter of sainthood (wilāyah): whoever is granted dhikr has been granted that charter, and whoever is deprived of dhikr has been dismissed from it.

f: How did Ibn Kathīr interpret the verse "And the remembrance of Allah is greater" (29:45)?
b: It means Allah's remembrance of His servants is greater than their remembrance of Him.

f: What subtle linguistic point does Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī derive from the verse "And the remembrance of Allah is greater"?
b: The verse does not specify what it is greater than, indicating that Allah's remembrance possesses absolute greatness, just as "Allāhu Akbar" affirms greatness that belongs to Allah alone.

f: Which hadith is cited to show that Allah is the companion of those who remember Him?
b: "I am the companion (or intimate companion) of the one who remembers Me."

f: In the narration about Mūsā, what did Allah reply when Mūsā asked whether He was near or far?
b: Allah replied: "O Mūsā, I am the companion of the one who remembers Me."

f: According to another narration, how did Allah answer Mūsā's question about His nearness?
b: Allah said: "I am behind you, before you, to your right, and to your left. I am with My servant when he remembers Me, and I am with him when he calls upon Me."

f: According to one of the gnostic scholars quoted by the author, what is the first step when Allah wishes to befriend a servant?
b: Allah opens for him the door of dhikr (remembrance).

f: What spiritual progression is described after the door of dhikr is opened?
b: The servant tastes sweetness in dhikr, then Allah opens the door of nearness, raises him to the assemblies of intimacy, seats him upon the throne of tawḥīd, removes the veils, admits him into the station of singularity (fardāniyyah), unveils His Majesty and Grandeur, and the servant is freed from self-awareness and the claims of the ego.

f: What is fardāniyyah as explained in the commentary?
b: It is a Sufi term referring to a high rank among the friends of Allah (awliyāʾ), derived from the hadith of "the mufarridūn"—those who greatly remember Allah.

f: Which hadith is cited as the basis for the concept of fardāniyyah?
b: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The mufarridūn have gone ahead." When asked who they were, he replied: "The men who remember Allah often and the women who remember Allah often."

f: What did Shaykh ʿAlī al-Marṣafī say is the greatest and quickest means for a seeker to reach Allah?
b: He said the shaykhs found no remedy greater or quicker than constant perseverance in the remembrance of Allah (dhikr).

f: How did Shaykh ʿAlī al-Marṣafī compare the effect of dhikr on the heart?
b: Dhikr polishes the heart like a polishing stone burnishes copper, whereas other acts of worship are like soap cleaning copper.

f: What does the commentary intend by this comparison?
b: That dhikr is faster and more effective than other acts of worship in purifying, refining, and cleansing the heart.

f: Which Qur'anic verses are cited to show that remembering Allah causes the hearts of believers to tremble?
b: "The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned..." (8:2) and "Give glad tidings to the humble, whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned..." (22:34–35).

f: How does the commentary interpret the trembling (wajal) mentioned in these verses?
b: It indicates the polishing and purification of the heart through the remembrance of Allah.

f: Which Qur'anic verse is cited to show the powerful effect of Allah's remembrance upon hearts?
b: "Allah has sent down the best statement... the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah." (39:23).

f: Which Qur'anic verse states that hearts find tranquility through dhikr?
b: "Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest." (13:28).

f: According to al-Ālūsī, why do remembrance of Allah sometimes produce fear and at other times tranquility?
b: Different Divine Names produce different manifestations according to a person's spiritual readiness; thus dhikr may produce fear (wajal) at one time and tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah) at another.

f: According to one interpretation cited by al-Ālūsī, when does the gnostic experience fear and when does he experience tranquility?
b: He experiences fear when hearing the remembrance from other people, but tranquility when hearing it from Allah Himself.

f: What saying of Abū al-Dardāʾ is cited about the heart?
b: "Everything has a polish, and the polish of hearts is the remembrance of Allah."

f: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about the polish of hearts?
b: "Everything has a polish, and the polish of hearts is the remembrance of Allah. Nothing is more effective in saving a person from Allah's punishment than the remembrance of Allah."

f: What are the benefits of making every breath a guardian of dhikr?
b: Constant vigilance over one's breaths preserves continuous remembrance of Allah, making dhikr the greatest gateway to Allah.

f: What is described as the greatest gateway to Allah?
b: Dhikr (the remembrance of Allah).

f: What special characteristic of dhikr removes obstacles on the spiritual path?
b: Dhikr unveils the veils that prevent entry into the Divine Presence.

f: What happens after a seeker's first veil is lifted through dhikr?
b: The seeker ascends to a higher station, seeks the next station above it, and continues progressing until reaching spiritual perfection.

f: Why does one who advances through dhikr progress more rapidly than one relying primarily on other acts of worship?
b: Dhikr removes veils quickly, whereas other acts often leave a person attached to a particular station for a long time because of the persistence of those veils.

f: According to the text, what is said about those who adhere to dhikr?
b: It is rare for someone who truly adheres to dhikr not to attain spiritual arrival (wuṣūl).

f: Which form of dhikr does the text describe as especially effective?
b: Dhikr of the heart (al-dhikr al-qalbī).

f: How does the text describe heart-dhikr?
b: It is witnessing, nearness, presence, and proximity to Allah.

f: What transformation does true heart-dhikr produce?
b: It replaces absence with presence and causes the one remembering to become annihilated (fanāʾ) in the One remembered.

f: Why does the text insist that dhikr should be received through the instruction (talqīn) of a perfected shaykh?
b: Because the secrets of the Divine Names are unveiled through the transmission of the Prophet ﷺ and then through his successors in an unbroken chain.

f: How are the secrets of Allah's Names transmitted according to the text?
b: Through instruction from the Prophet ﷺ, then through his successors, generation after generation, in a continuous spiritual chain.

f: According to the text, can someone attain complete spiritual perfection by practicing dhikr independently without receiving instruction from a shaykh?
b: No. Even if one performs abundant dhikr day and night independently, one does not attain the rank of the perfected unless guided by a realized spiritual master.

f: What minimum benefit does a disciple receive by taking dhikr from a perfected shaykh and entering his spiritual chain?
b: When the disciple stirs the chain through dhikr, the spirits of the shaykhs respond in succession up to the Prophet ﷺ and ultimately to the Divine Presence.

f: What is said about one who does not receive dhikr through the shaykhs or enter their spiritual chain?
b: None of the shaykhs respond to him, and his dhikr does not activate their spiritual chain throughout his lifetime.

f: What is presented as the benefit of receiving dhikr by talqīn (instruction)?
b: It connects the disciple to the spiritual chain (silsilah), through which the spirits of the shaykhs respond.

f: What should a person verify before taking a pledge (ʿahd) from a shaykh?
b: That the shaykh's creed ('aqīdah) is sound.

f: What should a seeker do after becoming confident in a shaykh's creed and faith?
b: Take the pledge from him, learn under him, and progress with him through the stages of the spiritual path.

f: How does the text describe the search for a perfected spiritual guide?
b: It is part of striving (jihād) to purify the soul and draw nearer to Allah.

f: Which statement of Ibn Sīrīn does the text cite regarding choosing a teacher?
b: "This knowledge is religion, so look carefully from whom you take your religion."

f: What is necessary besides dhikr to attain spiritual opening (fatḥ)?
b: Observing the proper etiquette (ādāb) of dhikr.

f: Why is dhikr alone said to be insufficient for attaining spiritual opening?
b: Because every act of worship without its proper etiquette yields little benefit.

f: What did the shaykhs unanimously agree that worship alone achieves?
b: It earns reward and entry into Paradise.

f: According to the text, what is required to attain Allah's special Presence?
b: Accompanying worship with proper spiritual etiquette (adab).

f: What is the primary goal of the spiritual path according to the text?
b: Nearness to Allah's special Presence and intimate companionship with Him without a veil.

f: How does the text describe the value of heavenly reward compared with nearness to Allah?
b: It likens reward to fodder for animals in comparison with the supreme goal of nearness to Allah.

f: How does the text describe the transmission of talqīn (instruction in dhikr)?
b: As a light flowing from the Prophet ﷺ to the Companions, then to the Followers, then through successive generations until the final recipient.

f: What does the text identify as the Sufi spiritual chain (silsilah)?
b: The continuous transmission of dhikr through successive teachers from the Prophet ﷺ.

f: According to the narration cited from Ibn ʿAjībah, through whom was the dhikr "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" transmitted after ʿAlī?
b: From ʿAlī to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, then to Ḥabīb al-ʿAjamī, Dāwūd al-Ṭāʾī, Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, al-Sirrī, al-Junayd, and then to the later masters of spiritual training.

f: According to the text, what is the only entrance to Allah?
b: The door of dhikr.

f: What does the text say is obligatory regarding dhikr?
b: One should occupy one's time with it and exert one's utmost effort in it.

f: What spiritual state should be observed in gatherings of dhikr?
b: Proper etiquette, sincerity, presence of heart, and annihilation in the One remembered.

f: What should be the seeker's ultimate goal during dhikr?
b: Allah's pleasure alone, without seeking anything besides Him.

f: How does the text describe the value of Paradise and Hell compared to pure love of Allah?
b: They are beneath the station of love, perfect faith, acceptance, contentment, and singleness of purpose.

f: What does the phrase "O Allah, You are my goal and Your pleasure is what I seek" express?
b: Sincere devotion in which Allah's pleasure alone is the seeker's objective.

f: What famous saying attributed to Rābiʿah al-ʿAdawiyyah does the text quote?
b: "I did not worship You out of fear of Your Fire or hope for Your Paradise, but because I found You worthy of worship."

f: According to the text, what is the highest realization of tawḥīd in worship?
b: Worshipping Allah because He is worthy of worship, with His pleasure as the sole aim.

f: How does the text interpret the hadith "I am the companion of the one who remembers Me"?
b: It refers to remembering Allah with proper etiquette and presence until the veils are lifted and the servant witnesses himself before his Lord.

f: What is meant by being Allah's "companion" (jalīs) according to the text?
b: Remaining in a state of spiritual witnessing and presence before Allah.

f: What causes a servant to leave Allah's special Presence according to the text?
b: Losing the state of spiritual witnessing and presence.

f: Does the text understand Allah's "Presence" as a physical place?
b: No. It explicitly denies that Allah is contained by any place, whether in the heavens or the earth.

f: According to Imām al-Nawawī, what is the primary objective of dhikr?
b: The presence of the heart (ḥuḍūr al-qalb).

f: What should a person strive to attain while making dhikr?
b: Presence of heart, reflection upon the words of dhikr, and understanding their meaning.

f: Why should the meanings of dhikr be contemplated?
b: Because reflection (tadabbur) is the intended objective of dhikr, just as it is in Qur'anic recitation.

f: Why does al-Nawawī recommend prolonging the phrase "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: Because prolonging it facilitates reflection and contemplation.

f: How does the text summarize the purpose of the entire chapter?
b: It is to witness Allah during dhikr.

f: To which station does the text relate witnessing Allah in dhikr?
b: The station of iḥsān.

f: How does the text describe the station of iḥsān?
b: "To worship Allah as though you see Him; if you do not see Him, He surely sees you."

f: How does the text describe the witnessing sought in dhikr?
b: As certain witnessing free from veils and inner obstacles, with the heart wholly absorbed in Allah.

f: How does the text qualify contemplation of Allah's Essence?
b: Without asking how (bilā kayf), without assigning a place (bilā ayna), and without likening or comparing Him to creation.

f: How does the text define rābiṭah in its simplest form?
b: As an imagined companionship (ṣuḥbah khayāliyyah) or heartfelt recollection.

f: What practical example does the text give to illustrate rābiṭah?
b: Like a Muslim far from ʿArafah connecting his heart to the pilgrims there, or a lover remembering the beloved.

f: What is the ultimate purpose of rābiṭah according to the text?
b: To train the heart to be attached to Allah, humble itself before Him, and maintain continual presence with Him while following His commands and prohibitions.

f: According to the text, with whom should the heart remain present in rābiṭah?
b: With Allah through witnessing, with the Messenger ﷺ through following his Sunnah, and with the shaykh through attentive remembrance as one's teacher and guide.

f: How is presence with Allah achieved according to the text?
b: Through witnessing (shuhūd) and vigilance (murāqabah).

f: How is presence with the Messenger ﷺ achieved?
b: By adopting his noble character, following his Sunnah, observing his etiquette, and fulfilling the rights owed to him as a member of his Ummah.

f: How does the text describe rābiṭah with the shaykh?
b: By binding the heart to him and keeping him in one's thoughts as a teacher and guide.

f: What analogy does the text use to explain rābiṭah with the shaykh?
b: Like a student remaining attached to the lessons of his teacher in order to learn and retain the method.

f: Why does the text say that remembering the shaykh benefits the disciple?
b: It strengthens resolve, encourages learning, imitation, and proper conduct even in the shaykh's absence.

f: Which hadith does the text cite to support maintaining the spiritual state experienced in the Prophet's ﷺ presence?
b: The hadith to Ḥanẓalah: "If you remained as you are when you are with me... the angels would shake hands with you... but, O Ḥanẓalah, an hour and an hour."

f: How does the text interpret the verse, "Fear Allah and be with the truthful" (Qur'an 9:119)?
b: It explains "being with the truthful" as both physical and spiritual companionship, the latter being rābiṭah.

f: What benefit does the text attribute to rābiṭah with the shaykh?
b: It helps preserve the disciple's etiquette, allows spiritual benefit during the shaykh's absence, increases spiritual illumination, and restrains base actions.

f: According to the text, what should one contemplate regarding the shaykh during rābiṭah?
b: His spiritual rank, nearness to Allah, striving, adherence to the Sharīʿah, and conformity to Sunni belief—not merely his physical form.

f: What doctrinal foundation does the text state for the Naqshbandī path?
b: The creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah and strict adherence to the rulings of the Sharīʿah.

f: How does the text define rābiṭah among the Sufis in general?
b: The disciple's inward gaze toward the spirituality of the shaykh while inclining to him with sincere love.

f: Is the concept of rābiṭah described as unique to the Naqshbandī order?
b: No. The text states that rābiṭah, in the meaning described, is found among all Sufis.

f: Which scholars are cited as discussing concepts related to rābiṭah?
b: The text cites scholars from all four Sunni schools, including al-Zamakhsharī, al-Ghazālī, Ibn Ḥajar, al-Suyūṭī, al-Shaʿrānī, al-Jurjānī, ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Jīlānī, Ibn al-Qayyim, Khalīl, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mursī, Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, and others.

f: How does the text describe the role of rābiṭah in the spiritual path?
b: It is an experiential means (wasīlah), not an independent end or objective.

f: Which Qur'anic verse does the text cite in connection with rābiṭah as a spiritual means?
b: "O you who believe, fear Allah and seek the means (wasīlah) to Him." (Qur'an 5:35).

f: Into how many types do the Naqshbandī shaykhs divide rābiṭah?
b: Two: rābiṭah in the presence of the shaykh and rābiṭah in the shaykh's absence.

f: How is rābiṭah performed when the shaykh is physically present?
b: The disciple directs his heart with sincere love toward the shaykh's heart in complete surrender until he becomes absorbed and forgets his own qualities in those of the shaykh.

f: How is rābiṭah performed when the shaykh is absent?
b: The disciple imagines the shaykh before his eyes, directs his attention to the shaykh's spirituality through that image, and continues until spiritual absence (ghaybah) or attraction (jadhbah) occurs.

f: What should the disciple do after experiencing ghaybah or jadhbah during rābiṭah?
b: He should stop the rābiṭah.

f: What spiritual transformation is said to occur after stopping rābiṭah?
b: The disciple becomes annihilated (fanāʾ) from his own self and qualities in the image of the shaykh.

f: What does the disciple witness after becoming annihilated in the image of the shaykh?
b: He witnesses the shaykh's spiritual perfections manifested in that image.

f: Why is the shaykh's spirituality said to be able to educate the disciple?
b: Because the shaykh's spiritual perfections are conveyed through his spirituality, which nurtures and trains the disciple.

f: What is the final goal of rābiṭah according to the text?
b: That the shaykh's spirituality gradually leads the disciple to Allah until he becomes one of those who have spiritually arrived (al-wāṣilīn al-kāmilīn).

f: According to the author, what practical role does the shaykh have in the Naqshbandi path?
b: The shaykh is described as a means of guidance who trains the disciple upon the Muhammadan Sharīʿah through his advice, example, and instruction. The disciple is expected to follow the shaykh's guidance in belief and conduct, while the shaykh himself is only a means (wasīlah) of guidance, not an end in himself.

f: How does the commentary explain the Qur'anic basis for using a spiritual means (wasīlah)?
b: It cites the verse, "Seek the means (wasīlah) to Him" (Qur'an 5:35), arguing that the disciple first benefits from observing and learning from the shaykh before progressing spiritually toward direct presence with Allah. It also notes that scholars such as al-Kawtharī cited this verse in support of the concept of rābiṭah.

f: According to the commentary, why is the spiritual intermediary (the shaykh) not intended to remain permanent?
b: Once the disciple has learned to maintain presence of heart with Allah and has progressed spiritually, there is no need to remain attached to the shaykh in the earlier manner. The disciple advances from attachment through love to attachment through following the Prophet ﷺ, in accordance with the verse: "Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you." (Qur'an 3:31).

f: What explanation does ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Nābulusī give regarding spiritual intermediaries?
b: Al-Nābulusī states that although direct awareness of Allah without any intermediary is the more perfect state, beginners normally cannot attain it immediately. Therefore, they require a spiritual means (wasīlah) that helps them distinguish experientially between the created and the Creator. Once they mature spiritually, the intermediary falls away.

f: According to the commentary, how does the disciple's spiritual progression develop?
b: The disciple first learns to keep his heart present with the shaykh whom he personally knows. He then advances to contemplating the Messenger ﷺ, whose noble qualities he knows though he has not seen him. Finally, he directs his heart to Allah Himself.

f: According to the author, what is the effect of rābiṭah even when the shaykh and disciple are physically far apart?
b: The author states that rābiṭah spiritually connects the disciple to the shaykh regardless of physical distance, whether one is in the East and the other in the West, allowing spiritual benefit and influence despite separation.

f: According to the author, can spiritual benefit be received from deceased saints through rābiṭah?
b: Yes. The author claims that both living and deceased perfected saints may spiritually benefit others through rābiṭah because the disciple comes under the influence of the saint's spiritual authority (wilāyah), through which divine spiritual perfections and manifestations are conveyed.

f: According to the author, does the disciple need to be consciously aware of this spiritual influence for it to occur?
b: No. The author explicitly states that this spiritual influence occurs whether the disciple recognizes it or not.

f: According to the author, why is rābiṭah considered one of the closest paths to Allah?
b: The author argues that rābiṭah is among the nearest means of reaching Allah because all other spiritual practices depend upon it for their special spiritual effects to appear, especially within the Naqshbandī path.

f: Why does the author say the Naqshbandī path is called "the path of rābiṭah"?
b: Because, according to the author, every aspect of spiritual practice in the Naqshbandī method depends upon rābiṭah accompanying it, without which those practices do not produce their intended spiritual benefit.

f: According to the author, what is the relationship between love (maḥabbah) and rābiṭah?
b: The author states that rābiṭah is fundamentally a form of love. Whoever lacks love for the spiritual guide lacks true rābiṭah.

f: According to the author, why is love considered essential for receiving spiritual benefit?
b: Because the author teaches that spiritual training (tarbiyah) and receiving spiritual overflow (istifāḍah) depend upon the existence of rābiṭah, which itself depends upon love. Without it, the disciple cannot receive those spiritual benefits, even if he were to accompany great righteous figures.

f: According to the author, with whom is rābiṭah spiritually beneficial?
b: The author states that rābiṭah is beneficial only when practiced with a perfect human being (al-insān al-kāmil) who possesses spiritual authority (wilāyah). He describes such a person as a mirror reflecting the Divine, such that one who contemplates the saint's spiritual reality with inner insight witnesses signs of Allah through it.

f: Into what two categories does the author divide rābiṭah?
b: The author divides rābiṭah into two forms: rābiṭah with living spiritual guides and rābiṭah with deceased saints.

f: According to the author, how should a disciple prepare inwardly before practicing rābiṭah with a deceased saint?
b: The author says the disciple should detach himself from worldly attachments, free his inner self from natural distractions, empty his heart of acquired impressions and passing thoughts, and prepare it for spiritual receptivity.

f: According to the author, how is rābiṭah with a deceased saint performed?
b: The author instructs the disciple to imagine the saint's spiritual reality as a pure light beyond physical form and to keep that image present in the heart until spiritual benefit or one of the saint's spiritual states is received.

f: Why does the author believe rābiṭah with deceased saints can produce spiritual benefit?
b: The author holds that the spiritual realities of perfected saints are sources of divine spiritual outpourings (fuyūḍāt). Therefore, whoever opens his heart to them through rābiṭah will inevitably receive some of those spiritual blessings.

f: According to the author, what is the first etiquette when performing rābiṭah at the grave of a righteous person?
b: The author says one should first greet the occupant of the grave with salām before beginning the practice.

f: According to the author, where should a visitor stand when performing rābiṭah at a grave?
b: The author instructs the visitor to stand on the right side of the grave near the deceased's feet, placing the right hand over the left above the navel and lowering the head toward the chest.

f: According to the author, which Qur'anic passages should be recited during rābiṭah at a grave?
b: The author prescribes reciting Sūrat al-Fātiḥah, Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ eleven times, and Āyat al-Kursī once, then gifting the reward of those recitations to the deceased.

f: After completing the prescribed recitations at a grave, what does the author instruct the disciple to do?
b: The author says the disciple should sit near the grave and direct his attention toward the spiritual reality of the deceased with the intention of receiving spiritual benefit (istifāḍah).

f: According to the author, can spiritual benefit be sought from the Prophet ﷺ without physically visiting Madinah?
b: Yes. The author states that a person who directs himself from wherever he is toward the spiritual reality of the Prophet ﷺ in his blessed grave in Madinah may receive spiritual benefit.

f: According to the author, does the same principle apply to other righteous saints?
b: Yes. The author states that one may likewise direct oneself from afar toward the spiritual realities of righteous saints in their graves and receive spiritual benefit from them.

f: According to the author, is physical travel necessary for spiritual benefit through rābiṭah?
b: No. The author concludes that rābiṭah itself, even without physically traveling to the grave, is sufficient for receiving spiritual benefit (istifāḍah) according to his understanding.

f: According to the author, what happens if rābiṭah is combined with focused spiritual attention (tawajjuh)?
b: The author says that combining rābiṭah with tawajjuh produces even greater spiritual illumination, describing it as "light upon light."

f: According to the author, what determines the effectiveness of rābiṭah?
b: The author states that its effectiveness depends upon the strength of the rābiṭah, not merely its outward performance.

f: According to the author, what is the result of consistently maintaining a strong rābiṭah?
b: The author claims that whoever perseveres in rābiṭah acquires all the spiritual states of the ṭarīqah and the perfections of spiritual realization (ḥaqīqah).

f: According to the author, what are the consequences of a weakened or broken rābiṭah?
b: The author states that when rābiṭah becomes deficient, spiritual transmission (istifāḍah) is interrupted, the disciple fails to attain the stages of spiritual wayfaring (sulūk), and the secrets of spiritual arrival are not disclosed to him.

f: According to the author, when does a disciple need rābiṭah?
b: The author says that the disciple needs rābiṭah only when he is unable to receive spiritual benefit directly from Allah without an intermediary.

f: According to the author, what should a disciple do if he becomes capable of receiving directly from Allah without an intermediary?
b: The author says that once a disciple reaches that state, he should leave rābiṭah, because the intermediary is no longer needed.

f: Why does the author say a spiritually advanced disciple should abandon rābiṭah?
b: The author argues that continuing rābiṭah after attaining direct reception from Allah would mean choosing a lower spiritual station over a higher one, preferring the level of intermediary (ḥijāb) over the station of direct witnessing (shuhūd).

f: How does the author describe persisting in rābiṭah after direct spiritual realization has been attained?
b: The author describes it as choosing descent instead of ascent and preferring the rank of veiling over direct witnessing, calling it a turning away from Allah.

f: According to the author, should the disciple completely sever his connection with the shaykh after leaving rābiṭah?
b: No. Although the author says the practice of rābiṭah should cease once direct reception is attained, he insists that the disciple should continue preserving his spiritual connection (nisbah) with the shaykh.

f: According to the author, what benefit remains in preserving one's spiritual connection (nisbah) with the shaykh?
b: The author states that maintaining the nisbah increases the disciple's spiritual witnessing, draws him nearer to the station of intimacy (uns) with Allah, and aids him in spiritual conversation (muḥādathah).

f: How does the commentary explain the author's instruction to leave rābiṭah?
b: The commentary explains that once a disciple reaches mature spiritual presence with Allah and perfect inward attentiveness, he should no longer remain occupied with the intermediary, because he has passed beyond the means and reached the One sought through that means.

f: According to the author, what are the two principal methods of dhikr practiced in the Naqshbandī tradition?
b: The author states that the Naqshbandī path employs two principal forms of dhikr: the remembrance of the Divine Name ("Allah"), which he calls Ism al-Dhāt (the Name of the Divine Essence), and the remembrance of the formula "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" (negation and affirmation).

f: Which Qur'anic verses does the commentary cite to demonstrate the importance of remembering Allah frequently?
b: The commentary cites verses commanding abundant remembrance of Allah, including: "Remember Allah as you remember your forefathers—or with even greater remembrance" (2:200), "Do not let your wealth or your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah" (63:9), "The men and women who remember Allah often—for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward" (33:35), "To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it" (35:10), and "Men whom neither trade nor commerce distracts from the remembrance of Allah" (24:37).

f: According to the commentary, what is meant by Ism al-Dhāt (the Name of the Divine Essence)?
b: The commentary explains that Ism al-Dhāt refers to the Divine Name "Allah," which uniquely designates Allah Himself and serves as the proper name of the Divine Essence.

f: According to the commentary, how does the name "Allah" relate to the other Beautiful Names (al-Asmāʾ al-Ḥusnā)?
b: The commentary states that all of Allah's Beautiful Names are attributed to the name "Allah." One may say that al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are names of Allah, but one does not say that "Allah" is a name of al-Raḥmān, indicating the comprehensive nature of the Divine Name.

f: Which hadith does the commentary cite concerning Allah's Beautiful Names?
b: The commentary cites the well-known hadith: "Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one; whoever enumerates (or preserves) them will enter Paradise." (Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.)

f: What linguistic disagreement do scholars mention regarding the name "Allah"?
b: The commentary notes that scholars differed over whether the name "Allah" is derived from another word (mushtaq) or non-derived (ghayr mushtaq).

f: Which scholars are mentioned as holding that the name "Allah" is not derived from another word?
b: The commentary attributes the view that "Allah" is non-derived to scholars including al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Sībawayh, a number of leading linguists, Imām al-Shāfiʿī, al-Khaṭṭābī, Imām al-Ḥaramayn al-Juwaynī, and others who agreed with them.

f: What linguistic argument is given for the view that the name "Allah" is non-derived?
b: The commentary argues that because the definite article (al-) is an inseparable part of the name, one says "Yā Allāh" rather than "Yā al-Allāh," whereas with other names such as al-Raḥmān the grammatical behavior differs. This is presented as evidence that the name is not derived from another root.

f: What explanation does Shaykh ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Saʿdī give regarding the name "Allah"?
b: Al-Saʿdī explains that the name "Allah" encompasses all attributes of perfection and majesty. According to the view he considers strongest, the word originally derives from al-Ilāh, and the name "Allah" comprehensively includes all of the Beautiful Names and exalted Divine Attributes.

f: According to Ibn al-Qayyim, what does the Divine Name "Allah" signify?
b: Ibn al-Qayyim states that the name "Allah" indicates all of the Beautiful Names (al-Asmāʾ al-Ḥusnā) and all of the perfect Divine Attributes through the three forms of indication recognized in Arabic legal theory: direct correspondence (muṭābaqah), inclusion (taḍammun), and necessary implication (iltizām).

f: What two important observations does Abū al-Baqāʾ al-Futūḥī make about the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: He states that (1) "Allah" is the proper name of the Divine Essence and therefore encompasses all of Allah's Beautiful Names, and (2) according to the majority of scholars it is the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam) by which Allah is described with every perfection and praise.

f: What does al-Shirbīnī say about the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: Al-Shirbīnī states that many leading scholars considered "Allah" to be the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam) and notes that it appears approximately 2,360 times in the Qur'an.

f: Which opinion does Imām Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ reportedly hold regarding the Greatest Name of Allah?
b: According to a narration transmitted from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan and cited by Ibn Amīr al-Ḥājj, Imām Abū Ḥanīfah رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ held that the Greatest Name of Allah is the name "Allah." The same opinion is attributed to al-Ṭaḥāwī, many scholars, and numerous spiritual masters.

f: Which Qur'anic verses does the commentary cite concerning the declaration "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: The commentary cites verses including: "We sent no messenger before you except that We revealed to him: There is no deity except Me, so worship Me." (21:25), "Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him..." (3:18), and "Allah presents the example of a good word like a good tree..." (14:24), interpreting the "good word" as the testimony of faith.

f: Which hadiths does the commentary cite concerning the virtue of saying "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: It cites several hadiths, including: "Faith has over sixty (or seventy) branches; the highest of them is saying 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh,'" "No servant says 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh' and dies upon it except that he enters Paradise," "The happiest people with my intercession are those who sincerely say 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh,'" and the hadith describing people removed from the Fire because they possessed even the smallest amount of faith alongside the testimony.

f: According to the author, why do some Naqshbandī masters prefer the dhikr of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: The author says they prefer it because of hadiths describing it as the best form of remembrance, because the Prophet ﷺ and the previous prophets proclaimed it, because it renews faith, and because they believe it has a particularly powerful effect in purifying and illuminating the inner self.

f: Which hadith does the author cite to support the superiority of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" as dhikr?
b: The author cites the hadith: "The best remembrance is 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh.'"

f: Which hadith does the author cite concerning the message shared by all the prophets?
b: The author cites the hadith: "The best thing that I and the prophets before me have said is: 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh.'"

f: Which hadith does the author cite regarding renewing faith?
b: The author cites the hadith: "Renew your faith by saying 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh.'"

f: According to the author, what spiritual effect does the formula "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" have?
b: The author claims that it has a uniquely powerful effect in purifying the inner self (bāṭin) and illuminating the heart, beyond that of other forms of dhikr.

f: According to the author, which form of dhikr do some other spiritual masters prefer instead?
b: The author says that some masters, including Muḥyī al-Dīn and other accomplished spiritual authorities, preferred the repeated remembrance of the Divine Name "Allah" (Ism al-Jalālah).

f: What Qur'anic evidence does the author cite for preferring the repetition of the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: The author cites the verse: "Say: 'Allah,' then leave them to indulge in their vain discourse." (Qur'an 6:91), presenting it as evidence for the remembrance of the Divine Name alone.

f: According to the author, why do some Naqshbandī masters prefer the dhikr of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: The author says they prefer it because the Prophet ﷺ described it as the best form of remembrance, because it was the central proclamation of all the prophets, because it renews faith, and because they believe it has a uniquely powerful effect in purifying and illuminating the heart.

f: Which hadith does the author cite to describe "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" as the best form of remembrance?
b: The author cites the hadith: "The best remembrance (dhikr) is 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh,' and the best supplication is 'Al-ḥamdu lillāh.'"

f: Which hadith does the author cite concerning the greatest statement uttered by all the prophets?
b: The author cites the hadith: "The best thing that I and the prophets before me have said is: 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh, alone without partner.'"

f: Which hadith does the author cite about renewing one's faith?
b: The author cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Renew your faith." When asked how, he replied: "Increase your saying of 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh.'"

f: According to the commentary, what does the hadith of the "card" (biṭāqah) illustrate about the testimony of faith?
b: The commentary cites the hadith in which a servant's record of sins is outweighed by a card bearing the testimony "Ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh wa anna Muḥammadan ʿabduhu wa rasūluh." It concludes with the statement: "Nothing outweighs the Name of Allah."

f: According to the commentary, what reward is mentioned for sincerely saying "Lā ilāha illā Allāh"?
b: The commentary cites the hadith stating that whoever sincerely says "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" has the gates of Heaven opened for it until it reaches the Throne.

f: According to Imām al-Junayd, what is the state of one who remembers the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: Al-Junayd describes such a person as forgetful of himself, connected to his Lord, fulfilling His rights, contemplating Him with his heart, while the lights of direct witnessing burn away the qualities of his human ego.

f: According to one opinion cited by the author, how should a disciple choose between the dhikr of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" and the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: The author says that if the disciple finds greater spiritual effect in "Lā ilāha illā Allāh," he should persist in it, whereas if he finds greater effect in remembering the Divine Name "Allah," he should continue with that instead.

f: According to another opinion cited by the author, whose instruction should determine the disciple's form of dhikr?
b: The author states that some scholars hold the disciple should engage in whichever form of dhikr his shaykh instructs him to practice.

f: According to another opinion cited by the author, what guidance should be given after the disciple has learned the method of dhikr?
b: The author says that once the disciple understands the proper method, he may choose whichever form of dhikr best protects him from distraction (tafriqah) and most gathers his heart into spiritual concentration (jamʿiyyah).

f: According to the author, what criterion should determine which form of dhikr a disciple continues practicing?
b: The author says the disciple should continue with the form of dhikr that most effectively gathers the heart, minimizes distraction, and produces the strongest spiritual influence.

f: According to the author, which form of dhikr is generally more effective for spiritual ascent?
b: Although he presents multiple opinions, the author concludes that the dhikr of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" (negation and affirmation) is generally more conducive to spiritual ascent (taraqqī) and to increasing the light of the heart.

f: According to the author, what did Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi recommend regarding the remembrance (dhikr) of Allah?
b: Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi advised: "Let your remembrance be 'Allah, Allah,' for this Name is the sovereign of all the Divine Names."

f: According to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi, why is the Divine Name "Allah" considered the "sovereign of the Names"?
b: Because it encompasses all the meanings contained in "Lā ilāha illā Allāh," including beliefs, knowledge, spiritual etiquette, and realities.

f: According to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi, what is the foundation (bisāṭ) and fruit (thamara) of the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: Its foundation is knowledge (`ilm), and its fruit is spiritual light (nūr).

f: According to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi, is spiritual light (nūr) itself the ultimate objective of dhikr?
b: No. Spiritual light is not sought for its own sake but because it leads to unveiling (kashf) and direct witnessing (ʿiyān).

f: According to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi, why should one frequently repeat the Divine Name "Allah"?
b: Because it contains all the meanings of "Lā ilāha illā Allāh," making it preferable to other forms of dhikr for those capable of it.

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, why is the Name "Allah" called the "Sultan of the Divine Names"?
b: Because it is regarded as the Supreme Name (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam) and the chief among all the Divine Names.

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, how does remembrance of the Name "Allah" affect the seeker?
b: Through continual repetition, the remembrance permeates one's entire being until its lights spread through every part of the person.

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, through which stages does the remembrance of "Allah" progress within the seeker?
b: It moves from the tongue, to the heart, then to the spirit (rūḥ), and finally to the innermost secret (sirr).

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, what is the result when dhikr reaches the innermost secret (sirr)?
b: The tongue falls silent, and the seeker reaches witnessing (shuhūd) and direct vision (ʿiyān).

f: According to the author, what saying of Baha' al-Din Naqshband does he allude to?
b: "Our path is companionship (ṣuḥbah), and all good lies in gathering (jamʿiyyah)."

f: According to Imam al-Ghazali رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what does the verse "Say: Allah, then leave them in their vain discourse" (Qur'an 6:91) indicate spiritually?
b: It points to spiritual singleness (tafrīd) and detachment (tajrīd): remembering Allah alone while turning away from everything else.

f: According to Imam al-Ghazali رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what does the statement "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" ultimately mean in the spiritual sense?
b: It means that there is no true object of worship or ultimate love except Allah; every attachment besides Him is a form of bondage.

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, how should the command "Say: Allah, then leave them in their vain discourse" be understood spiritually?
b: It means to remember Allah until everything else disappears from one's awareness, then leave people occupied with their distractions.

f: According to Ibn 'Ajibah, what happens when one remembers Allah while observing His blessings?
b: The seeker becomes absorbed in witnessing Allah and no longer remains occupied with the blessings themselves.

f: According to some Sufi masters, when should a seeker continue using the formula "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" rather than the single Name "Allah"?
b: As long as the seeker still perceives created things (the cosmos), remembrance through negation and affirmation ("Lā ilāha illā Allāh") remains appropriate.

f: According to some Sufi masters, why is "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" regarded as especially suitable during the earlier stages of the path?
b: Because it is considered the key to the realities of the heart and a means of ascending toward the unseen.

f: According to some Sufi masters, when is it considered appropriate to remember Allah using only the single Name "Allah"?
b: After the seeker's ego, desires, and sense of separate identity have been annihilated (fanā'), making pure remembrance of the Divine Name appropriate.

f: According to the author, why do different Sufi masters recommend different forms of dhikr?
b: Because each form of remembrance is appropriate for different spiritual states and levels of the seeker; "each has its own orientation and spiritual path."

f: According to the Naqshbandi tradition described in the text, what should a seeker do before beginning dhikr?
b: Before beginning dhikr, the seeker should prepare himself outwardly and inwardly by observing the prescribed etiquette (adab), including purification, proper sitting, repentance, humility, and reflection on death.

f: According to the author, what sitting posture is recommended before beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker should sit on his knees in a posture opposite to the tawarruk posture used in prayer, while facing the qiblah.

f: According to the author, why does he recommend a sitting posture opposite to the tawarruk used in prayer?
b: So that no one mistakes this posture for an act of worship legislated as part of the prayer. It is merely a respectful sitting position for engaging in unrestricted dhikr, not a newly introduced ritual act.

f: According to the author, what state of ritual purity should a seeker have before beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker should be in a state of wuḍū' (ritual ablution).

f: According to the author, in which direction should the seeker face while beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker should face the qiblah.

f: According to the author, how many times should the seeker recite "Astaghfirullāh" before beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker should recite "Astaghfirullāh" either five, fifteen, or twenty-five times.

f: According to the author, how should the seeker recite "Astaghfirullāh" before dhikr?
b: It should be recited with the tongue while the heart is consciously engaged in the meaning.

f: According to the author, what inward attitude should accompany the initial istighfār before dhikr?
b: The seeker should regard himself as sinful, deficient, unworthy, and lacking righteous deeds.

f: According to the author, after recognizing his shortcomings, upon what should the seeker rely?
b: He should despair of relying upon his own deeds and instead place his trust in Allah and depend upon His grace and bounty.

f: According to the author, what should the seeker contemplate after making istighfār?
b: The seeker should contemplate death, the events surrounding it, and the terrors of the grave.

f: According to the author, how vividly should the seeker imagine death before beginning dhikr?
b: He should imagine that death has already come, that his final breath has arrived, and that he is about to leave this world.

f: According to the author, what events after death should the seeker mentally picture before dhikr?
b: He should imagine being washed, shrouded, carried on the funeral bier, buried in the grave, and left alone after people depart.

f: According to the author, what realization should the seeker reach while imagining himself in the grave?
b: He should realize that neither his wealth, deeds, nor family can benefit him, and that only Allah remains as his true support and protector.

f: According to the author, how should the seeker imagine standing before Allah during this meditation?
b: He should imagine himself standing before Allah with complete humility, helplessness, inadequacy, shame, and need.

f: According to the author, approximately how long should the seeker remain in this contemplation before beginning dhikr?
b: He should remain in this contemplation for approximately a quarter of an hour (about fifteen minutes).

f: According to the author's commentary, what are the two general categories of dhikr mentioned in the Qur'an and Sunnah?
b: The first is unrestricted (muṭlaq) dhikr, in which the manner is left open; the second is restricted (muqayyad) dhikr, whose wording, number, or manner has been specifically prescribed in revelation.

f: According to the author's commentary, what distinguishes unrestricted (muṭlaq) dhikr from restricted (muqayyad) dhikr?
b: Unrestricted dhikr allows personal effort in choosing its form, whereas restricted dhikr must be performed exactly as transmitted in the Qur'an or Sunnah to obtain its specific promised reward.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker recite after contemplating death?
b: The seeker should recite Sūrat al-Fātiḥah once and Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ three times.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, to whom should the reward of the recited Qur'an be dedicated?
b: The reward should be dedicated to the spirit of the Naqshbandi master, Khwāja Bahā' al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Uwaysī al-Bukhārī (Shāh Naqshband).

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker request from Bahā' al-Dīn Naqshband after dedicating the reward?
b: The seeker should inwardly seek spiritual assistance (istimdād) from him with the heart.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, how should the seeker visualize his own spiritual guide (murshid)?
b: He should visualize the spiritual image of his murshid between his eyebrows (at the forehead) and concentrate deeply upon it.

f: According to the author's commentary, what is the purpose of beginning Naqshbandi litanies with the testimony of faith and seeking forgiveness?
b: The purpose is to renew one's faith, repent from sins, and prepare the heart for sincere remembrance of Allah.

f: According to the author's commentary, what is the purpose of the meditation on death before dhikr?
b: It is to cultivate surrender to Allah, humility, poverty before Him, trust in Him, and detachment from worldly attachments.

f: According to the author's commentary, which Qur'anic verse is cited as evidence that believers may pray for those who passed before them?
b: The verse is: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith." (Qur'an 59:10).

f: According to the author's commentary, which Qur'anic verse is cited regarding righteous descendants being joined with believing ancestors?
b: The verse is: "Those who believed, and whose descendants followed them in faith—We shall join their descendants with them." (Qur'an 52:21).

f: According to the author's commentary, what principle of divine justice accompanies Allah's joining believing descendants with their ancestors?
b: Every person remains accountable only for his own deeds, as indicated by the continuation of Qur'an 52:21: "Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned."

f: According to Imam al-Nawawi رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, what is the well-known Shāfiʿī position regarding the reward of Qur'an recitation for the deceased?
b: The well-known Shāfiʿī position is that the reward of Qur'an recitation does not reach the deceased, although some Shāfiʿī scholars held that it does.

f: According to Imam al-Nawawi رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, which imam agreed that the reward of Qur'an recitation reaches the deceased?
b: Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held that its reward reaches the deceased.

f: According to Ibn Qudāmah, what evidence supports the view that the reward of Qur'an recitation benefits the deceased?
b: He argued that since authentic texts establish that fasting, ḥajj, supplication, and seeking forgiveness benefit the deceased, other righteous acts such as Qur'an recitation may also benefit them.

f: According to Ibn Qudāmah, what practice of the Muslim community did he cite as supporting the gifting of Qur'an recitation to the deceased?
b: He cited the widespread practice of Muslims throughout different lands and generations gathering to recite the Qur'an and dedicate its reward to their deceased without objection.

f: According to the Ḥanafī school, does the reward of Qur'an recitation reach the deceased?
b: Yes. The Ḥanafī school explicitly holds that the reward of Qur'an recitation may be gifted to and benefit the deceased.

f: According to Ibn Taymiyyah, what was his preferred opinion regarding gifting the reward of bodily acts of worship to the deceased?
b: Ibn Taymiyyah preferred the opinion that the rewards of bodily acts of worship—including prayer, fasting, and Qur'an recitation—may all reach the deceased.

f: According to the author, if the evidences for and against the deceased benefiting from gifted rewards were considered equal, which opinion should be preferred and why?
b: The author says the opinion that the reward reaches the deceased should be preferred because it accords with Allah's generosity, mercy, and kindness.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what is the visualization of one's spiritual guide called?
b: It is called the noble rābiṭah (spiritual connection).

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker do after visualizing the image of his spiritual guide?
b: He should place the imagined image into the center of his heart and keep it there while turning his complete attention inward.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, to what should the seeker direct all of his senses after establishing the rābiṭah?
b: He should direct all of his senses and complete attention toward his heart.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what meaning should the seeker contemplate in his heart during dhikr?
b: He should contemplate the meaning signified by the Divine Name "Allah"—namely, Allah's Divine Essence, without imagining any likeness or form.

f: According to the author, what does it mean to contemplate the Divine Name "Allah" correctly?
b: It means understanding the meaning indicated by the Name while avoiding any physical image, likeness, or anthropomorphic conception of Allah.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, with what should the seeker's heart be filled?
b: His heart should be filled with remembrance of the meaning indicated by the Divine Name "Allah."

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what is wuqūf qalbī (heart-attention)?
b: It is keeping the heart fully occupied with the remembrance of Allah and the meaning of His Name while maintaining complete awareness of the heart during dhikr.

f: According to the author, why is this practice called wuqūf qalbī (heart-attention)?
b: Because the seeker "stands" over his heart, watching it carefully and ensuring that it remains occupied with Allah's remembrance and is not distracted.

f: According to the author, when should wuqūf qalbī be maintained?
b: It should be maintained throughout the entire period of dhikr and, whenever possible, even outside the formal remembrance session.

f: According to the author, what rank does wuqūf qalbī hold among the practices of dhikr?
b: It is described as the greatest pillar (rukn al-aʿẓam) of dhikr.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what supplication should accompany wuqūf qalbī?
b: The seeker should say inwardly: "My God, You are my goal, and Your pleasure is what I seek." (Ilāhī anta maqṣūdī wa riḍāka maṭlūbī.)

f: According to the author, why should a person understand the meaning of the Divine Name he is remembering?
b: Because one should not engage in remembrance of a Name whose meaning, significance, or implications he does not understand or toward which he has neither hope, fear, nor sincere turning.

f: According to the commentary, what are the two meanings of wuqūf qalbī in the Naqshbandi tradition?
b: First, remaining continually present with Allah without heedlessness; second, keeping constant watch over one's own heart so that it remains occupied with Allah's remembrance and its meaning.

f: According to the commentary, how did ʿUbayd Allāh al-Aḥrār define wuqūf qalbī?
b: He defined it as directing one's attention to the heart during dhikr, keeping it occupied with both the words and meanings of the remembrance, and preventing it from becoming heedless or distracted.

f: According to the commentary, to which act of worship is wuqūf qalbī compared?
b: It is compared to khushūʿ (humble attentiveness) in prayer, where the servant turns completely toward Allah and becomes heedless of everything besides Him.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, how should the seeker begin the remembrance (dhikr) after completing the preliminary preparations?
b: He should begin remembering Allah inwardly by repeating the Divine Name "Allah, Allah, Allah" with the heart while maintaining wuqūf qalbī (heart-attention).

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, how should the heart be maintained during the repetition of the Divine Name?
b: The seeker should maintain wuqūf qalbī, keeping the heart fully attentive to Allah and as free from distracting thoughts as possible.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker strive to remove while engaged in dhikr?
b: He should strive to empty his heart of distracting thoughts (khawāṭir) as much as he is able.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what invocation should be repeated periodically during dhikr?
b: After every hundred repetitions—or sooner if desired—the seeker should inwardly repeat: "My God, You are my goal, and Your pleasure is what I seek" (Ilāhī anta maqṣūdī wa riḍāka maṭlūbī).

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker do if he enters a state of absorption or forgetfulness of the world during dhikr?
b: He should stop the verbal repetition and remain absorbed in that state while continuing wuqūf qalbī.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, when should the seeker resume repeating the Divine Name after entering a state of absorption?
b: He should resume the remembrance when he regains ordinary awareness of himself.

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, what should the seeker do immediately after completing the dhikr session?
b: He should remain quietly for a short time while maintaining wuqūf qalbī, awaiting any spiritual inspiration (wārid) and expecting divine spiritual effusion (fayḍ).

f: According to the Naqshbandi method described in the text, why should the seeker delay opening his eyes after completing dhikr?
b: Because subtle spiritual gifts or inspirations may descend during those few moments of stillness, even if he does not consciously perceive them.

f: According to the Qur'anic verses cited by the author, how should Allah be remembered inwardly?
b: Allah should be remembered inwardly with humility, reverence, fear, and without loudness of speech.

f: According to Qur'an 7:205, what warning accompanies the command to remember Allah inwardly?
b: The verse concludes: "Do not be among the heedless."

f: According to Imam Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, what does the phrase "Do not be among the heedless" imply regarding remembrance of Allah?
b: It implies that inward remembrance of Allah should be continual, so that a person strives not to become heedless of Allah even for a moment, according to human ability.

f: According to Imam Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, why does continual remembrance affect the soul?
b: Because there is a profound relationship between the soul and the body: repeated actions produce lasting spiritual dispositions, just as mental states influence the body.

f: According to al-Zamakhsharī, why is silent remembrance generally preferable to loud remembrance?
b: Because concealing one's remembrance is more conducive to sincerity (ikhlāṣ), deeper reflection, and spiritual presence.

f: According to al-Ālūsī, what is one benefit of remembering Allah inwardly?
b: Inward remembrance is more conducive to sincerity and therefore closer to acceptance by Allah.

f: According to Ibn al-Qayyim, what is the highest form of dhikr?
b: The highest form of dhikr is that in which both the heart and the tongue remember Allah together.

f: According to Ibn al-Qayyim, what is the second-highest form of dhikr?
b: The second-highest form is remembrance performed by the heart alone.

f: According to Ibn al-Qayyim, what is the third level of dhikr?
b: The third level is remembrance performed by the tongue alone, without the heart's participation.

f: What is the first etiquette before beginning dhikr according to the Naqshbandi manual?
b: Before beginning dhikr, the seeker should sit respectfully (in a reversed tawarruk-like posture), face the qiblah, be in a state of wudu if possible, and prepare inwardly for remembrance.

f: What role does istighfār (seeking forgiveness) play before beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker begins by saying "Astaghfirullāh" 5, 15, or 25 times with both tongue and heart while acknowledging personal sins, shortcomings, and complete dependence upon Allah's mercy rather than one's own deeds.

f: Why does the Naqshbandi manual recommend reflecting on death before dhikr?
b: The seeker imagines death, burial, separation from family, and standing alone before Allah so that attachment to worldly things is reduced and the heart becomes humble, sincere, and reliant upon Allah alone.

f: How long does the manual recommend contemplating death before dhikr?
b: It recommends maintaining this reflection for approximately a quarter of an hour.

f: What Qur'anic recitations are recommended before beginning dhikr?
b: The seeker recites Sūrat al-Fātiḥah once and Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ three times.

f: To whom is the reward of the opening Qur'anic recitations dedicated according to the manual?
b: Their reward is gifted to Shāh Bahāʾ al-Dīn Naqshband, the founder of the Naqshbandi order, while seeking spiritual benefit through him.

f: What is meant by the "honourable rābiṭah" (الرَّابِطَةُ الشَّرِيفَةُ) before dhikr?
b: It consists of imagining the spiritual image of one's spiritual guide between the eyebrows, concentrating upon it, and seeking spiritual benefit through that connection before beginning dhikr.

f: After visualizing the spiritual guide, what should the seeker do next?
b: The seeker imagines the guide's image within the heart, then turns complete attention toward the heart itself while contemplating the meaning signified by the Divine Name Allah.

f: What does the Naqshbandi manual mean by contemplating the Divine Name "Allah" during dhikr?
b: The seeker reflects upon the reality indicated by the Name—Allah Himself—without imagining any physical likeness or form, filling the heart with awareness of the One signified by the Name.

f: What is al-waqf al-qalbī (الْوُقُوفُ الْقَلْبِيُّ) according to the Naqshbandi tradition?
b: It is maintaining continuous awareness of the heart while keeping it occupied with both the remembrance of Allah and the meaning of the Divine Name. It is regarded as the central pillar of dhikr.

f: Is al-waqf al-qalbī required only during dhikr?
b: No. Although essential during dhikr, the manual recommends maintaining it outside formal sessions whenever possible.

f: What supplication does the seeker silently repeat before beginning the main dhikr?
b: The seeker says inwardly: "Ilāhī anta maqṣūdī wa riḍāka maṭlūbī" ("My God, You are my aim, and Your pleasure is what I seek.").

f: How is the Divine Name "Allah" remembered in the Naqshbandi method?
b: The Name "Allah" is repeated silently with the heart while maintaining continuous heart awareness (waqf qalbī) and striving to keep distracting thoughts away.

f: During silent dhikr, when is the supplication "Ilāhī anta maqṣūdī wa riḍāka maṭlūbī" repeated?
b: It is repeated inwardly approximately every hundred repetitions—or sooner if desired—while continuing the remembrance.

f: What should the seeker do if deep absorption or spiritual concentration occurs during dhikr?
b: If absorbed to the point that awareness of worldly matters fades, the seeker temporarily stops repeating the dhikr verbally or mentally and remains immersed in that state of inward awareness.
